adds.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Manisa included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised; marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military, and since 2015 authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49. The page records a February 2026 press report of legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison, which was not included in the 2026 omnibus (the 12th judicial package), and September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involving 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses.

adds.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
adds.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In June 2025 the health ministry's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but were ultimately not submitted to parliament.
